problem_text: Let n > 1 be a given integer. An n×n×n cube is composed of n^3 unit cubes. Each unit cube is painted with one colour. For each n×n×1 box consisting of n^2 unit cubes (in any of the three possible orientations), we consider the set of colours present in that box (each colour is listed only once). This way, we get 3n sets of colours, split into three groups according to the orientation. It happens that for every set in any group, the same set appears in both of the other groups. Determine, in terms of n, the maximal possible number of colours that are present.
solution_text: The answer is n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2. Key steps: (1) The matching condition implies that for each colour c, the set of x-layers, y-layers, and z-layers containing c are the same set L_c (after relabeling layers). (2) Each colour c needs at least |L_c| cubes forming a matching in L_c^3, and using exactly |L_c| is optimal. (3) Upper bound: for each t, colours with max(L_c)=t must be assigned to distinct cubes (t,j,k) with j,k in [t], giving at most t^2 such colours. (4) Summing: total colours <= sum of t^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. (5) Construction achieves this bound by tiling [n]^3 with matchings grouped by level.
solution_summary: The condition forces each colour to have identical layer-membership sets across all three orientations (A_c = B_c = C_c = L_c). Grouping colours by max(L_c) = t and counting available cube positions in layer t within [t]^2 gives a_t <= t^2. Summing yields the bound n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, achieved by a matching tiling construction.
structure_features: n×n×n cube with 3n layer colour-sets; symmetry condition across three orientations; optimization of colour count under matching constraint
key_insight: Group colours by max(L_c) = t; each such colour must occupy a distinct cube (t, j, k) with j, k <= t, giving at most t^2 colours per level
expected_ai_method: Direct incidence counting: compute sum of m_c = n^3 and try to maximize number of colours without structural insight
correct_method: Level decomposition: group colours by max(L_c), bound each level by t^2 via cube-position counting, sum to get n(n+1)(2n+1)/6

rounds.question: Describe the structure of this problem. What are the key objects, constraints, and what are we trying to optimize?
rounds.expected_answer: We have an n×n×n cube of n^3 unit cubes, each painted one colour. There are 3n layer colour-sets (n per orientation). The condition is that every colour-set in any orientation group also appears in both other groups. We want to maximize the total number of distinct colours.

rounds.question: List all possible approaches to bound the number of colours. What mathematical tools could be relevant?
rounds.expected_answer: Possible approaches: (1) Direct incidence counting between colours and layers, (2) Layer-by-layer analysis of colour-sets, (3) Colour-by-colour structural analysis examining what layers each colour appears in, (4) Algebraic methods using the symmetry condition, (5) Extremal arguments with constructions.

rounds.question: Try a direct counting approach: count the total number of colour-layer incidences. What bound does this give? Why is it insufficient?
rounds.expected_answer: Each colour c appears in m_c x-layers, m_c y-layers, and m_c z-layers. The total incidences sum to n^3 per orientation. So sum m_c = n^3. But this only gives number of colours <= n^3 (when all m_c=1), which is not tight. The m_c=1 case fails because the matching condition cannot be satisfied: all colours in one x-layer would need the same y-layer, limiting to at most n colours per layer.

rounds.question: For each colour c, what does the matching condition imply about its layer memberships across the three orientations? Can you show that the set of x-layers, y-layers, and z-layers containing c must be related?
rounds.expected_answer: The condition that every layer colour-set appears in all three groups means there exist permutations sigma, tau such that the colour-set of x-layer i equals that of y-layer sigma(i) equals that of z-layer tau(i). For colour c, this means c is in x-layer i iff c is in y-layer sigma(i) iff c is in z-layer tau(i). After relabeling, A_c = B_c = C_c =: L_c. So each colour has the same layer-membership set in all three orientations.

rounds.question: Given that each colour c has a layer set L_c, and its cubes form a matching in L_c^3, how can you bound the number of colours with max(L_c) = t for each t?
rounds.expected_answer: Colours with max(L_c) = t have L_c subset of [t] with t in L_c. Their cube in x-layer t is at position (t, j, k) with j, k in L_c subset [t], so (j,k) in [t]^2. There are t^2 such positions, each assigned to at most one colour. So the number of colours with max(L_c) = t is at most t^2.

rounds.question: Sum the per-level bounds to get the total upper bound. How can this bound be achieved by a construction?
rounds.expected_answer: Total colours <= sum_{t=1}^{n} t^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. The construction: for each level t, create t^2 colours with max(L_c) = t, assign each to a distinct cube (t, j, k) with j, k in [t], and extend each to a matching in L_c^3. The matchings tile [n]^3 by carefully choosing L_c subsets and matching structures.

rounds.question: You've found the answer. Summarize the key insight that made this problem tractable.
rounds.expected_answer: The key insight was the level decomposition by max(L_c). The structural observation that A_c = B_c = C_c = L_c transformed the global matching condition into a per-colour constraint. Then grouping colours by max(L_c) = t and counting available cube positions (t, j, k) with j, k <= t gave the tight per-level bound of t^2, summing to n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
